description.narrative: Reporting is an important management tool which is used to inform relevant government officials and other stakeholders about the results being achieved by individual projects and the programme as a whole. For project partners, it is compulsory to use the prescribed Orange Knowledge annual report format in order to report on project achievements. The annual report also provides valuable data on the financial situation of the project. Based on an analysis of the project performance in relation to the project output(s) and expected outcome(s), a revision of the project work plan may be suggested by the project partners. The consequences of a possible revision on the project work plan and budget must be made clear in the annual report. Nuffic monitors outputs and outcomes and not activities . Therefore, the main focus of the annual report must be on the achievement of the project’s output(s) and planned outcome(s). The information provided in the annual reports of the projects is used by Nuffic to monitor the progress of the project and to inform the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and other stakeholders about the output(s) and outcome(s) being achieved by individual projects and the Orange Knowledge programme as a whole. Please note that if project progress is in accordance with the original planning, reporting requirements are minimal. Only in case of deviations from the planning, more elaboration is demanded. In the grant award letter, the dates for submission of the annual reports are mentioned. In case of a three-year project, between 5-7 reports are obligatory. The first report (0) is a very short report which focuses on specific conditions and/or recommendations in the grant. There is no need to report on progress in achieving outputs and outcomes, which is done in the first annual report. As annex to the report 0, the consortium agreements between the partners should be submitted. The final report must reflect on the entire project period.

actual.value:
1. Choreography, improvisation and composition training Theater is primarily a means of communication. To communicate clearly one must develop the ability to use a 'language' and a clear grammar. Much attention is paid in the training to the search for one's own language to tell a story and is thereby trained in composition assignments and dramaturgy. 2. Didactic and pedagogical training About 25% of the time is spent on this part. When one is going to make a project with a group, it is important to pay attention to the communication with the group and the way of transferring the 'language' that one wants to develop. This in combination with analysis of body movement and anatomy. Also important is the fact that teacher training immediately broadens the market for work for the participants. giving a dance/theatre lesson opens up opportunities to market yourself at all kinds of (social) cultural centers. 3. Training/ Coaching in didactic approach of SRHR issues Each creative unit of makers has been talking to youngsters about the subject these young people felt urgent/important. All trainers have been coaching the group on dealing with attention and sensitivity and to create a safe environment in which all highschool students feel free to express themselves during rehearsals. 4. Intermediate contemporary dance training Technical skills an competences are acquired by daily physical training in every module. To master and memorize body movements is the basic to develop a grammar for storytelling. During dramaturgy and pedagogy training there has also been room for physical theatre and voice training. Storytelling consisted mostly of a combination of dance and theatre. 5. Intermediate urban dance techniques The trainer for this module was not available and these classes mostly concentrated on traditional dance vocabulary of burundi and urban dance impro's by some of the group members. They developed material with youngsters who were keen to use that kind of vocabulary. 6. Creating short presentations with youngsters The group has been divided in 6 creative units to work with sic different highschools in Bujumbura. Both private schools and public schools. The group itself made contact with the school principals and planned the rehearsals. After an audition they started working with a group of 15-20 young people. They worked with the group on Friday afternoon and Saturday morning. Each week, each school was visited by one of the trainers who coached the making process. After a rehearsal, there was an extensive evaluation of the development of the content (dramaturgy), the communication with the group and the training of the group. during weekdays, corrections were made to the material for storytelling with colleagues. Each creative unit had a number of dancers from the group at its disposal to make material that could then be studied with the young people. 7. Training in cultural entrepreneurship The training started with this part. The entire training was organized within the framework of organisation. Organizing schools and young people and a choreography is an organization of time and space. For that reason, it was good to start with a few days of entrepreneurial training that covered all aspects of making and selling a product. Another focus was also on the internal organization of the group with the formulation of multi-year goals, the division of tasks and fundraising. The training was given by a cultural entrepreneur from Uganda who was able to inform them well about the market in South East Africa and the specific complexity and possibilities.
In general the teams were free to choose a theme even one in which a teacher was staged as abusing a youngster in his class. None of the schoolheads were pressing the teams to change the story. Since the earlier work Les Larmes de Crocodile by Iivuga was censored during the period before election the group often discusses censorship. It has happened to other groups to be censored notably in the last edition of the Festival Buja Sans Tabu.
SRHR issues though are accepted to display. Sometimes there are comments about the strong position of women , but even gender based violence is accepted to discuss and to stage it in a graphic way.

comment.narrative: 15-08-2022: All 15 participants were part of the 2019 training "Acting for change"

title.narrative: B.O.1. Number of organisations strengthened by individual and/or group training

comment.narrative: 15-08-2022: All six participating schools have benefited from the skills gained from the training. Many school students gained new knowledge and schoolteachers were very interested in transforming social themes into a performance. All schools present the work outside the presented competition several times during cultural days or graduation ceremonies at their schools and some Irivuga members continued working with the students at the request of teachers. The trained group of Irivuga Art Company have especially learned new skills in the field of creating and organising. The degree of success of the production was determined by the extent to which each creative unit managed to organize itself well and to divide the work, as it had to be made in a short time. They progressed strongly in pedagogic and didactic skills of teaching art education. The team of LGC trainers/coaches has learned a lot about how to look and interpret meaning based on cultural sensitivity when shaping a story.

title.narrative: B.O.5. Number of organisations developed and implemented a gender strategy

comment.narrative: 16-08-2022: By definition, Le Grand Cru has an equal opportunity approach as a strategy for all trainers. Iriviga Art company does not have a special strategy but currently everyone is aware that women deserve equal opportunities. in the current organisational structure there are 4 leaders of which 2 men and 2 women.
